sentences.text: Jeholornis possessed a body size comparable to modern turkeys, featuring long tails and only a few small teeth.
Adult individuals reached a maximum length of 75 cm and weighed between 2.27 and 9.1 kg.
The species J. prima lacked teeth in the upper jaw and retained only three small teeth in the lower jaw.
Flight feathers found on the animal were asymmetrical and aerodynamic, reaching lengths of up to 21 centimeters.
A 2022 study identified Jeholornis prima as the earliest known fruit-eating bird, noting that it consumed the entire fruit rather than just the seeds.
One specimen was fossilized with gastroliths preserved inside its stomach.
The genus Jeholornis was described by Zhou and Zhang in 2002.
The holotype specimen of J. prima, cataloged as IVPP V13274, is held at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing.
More than 100 fossils have been discovered, but only seven have been formally described.
Jeholornis ate seeds from cycads, Ginkgo, or similar plants, and seeds measuring 8-10mm were found in the crop region of one fossil.
The ability to eat fruits likely developed when plants began developing new kinds of fruits around 135 million years ago, starting a co-evolutionary relationship about 120 million years ago.
Primitive avialans like Jeholornis could not achieve true flapping flight but were capable of semi-powered gliding or parachuting.
Examination of claw curvature and the presence of a reversed hallux suggest the bird may have been able to perch and spent much of its time in trees.
Juvenile specimens possessed more teeth than adults, suggesting they lost them as they matured.
The type species of the genus Jeholornis is J. prima, named for its primitive tail appearance.
The species J. palmapenis was described by O'Connor et al. in 2012, named for tail feathers arranged like palm leaves.
Zhou and Zhang classified Jeholornis as the type genus of the family Jeholornithidae and the order Jeholornithiformes.
Fossils were first found in the Jiufotang Formation in Hebei Province, China, where the animal lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages, between 125.77 and 113.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether the genus Jixiangornis is a synonym of Jeholornis, as a 2014 analysis suggested it might belong to short-tailed avialans instead.

A 2020 study concluded that Shenzhouraptor is a valid species distinct from Jeholornis prima, though it remains unknown whether Jeholornis and Shenzhouraptor represent the same genus or two distinct ones.
It is debated whether the reversed appearance of the hallux in Jeholornis is a true anatomical feature or an artifact of fossil crushing.
